Premise

A background
that pays attention.

The grid is decorative. It is also the only continuous element in the deck. What happens if we let it carry some of the meaning — not by saying anything, but by moving, breathing, attending.

Argument

Texture is information
delivered without ink.

A reader's eye treats density as emphasis long before it parses a word. If the grid concentrates where the headline lives and thins where the margin begins, the page is already telling you where to look. The text only confirms it.

This template uses that signal twice: once for entry, once for hierarchy. The same wave that loads the slide also draws the eye to whatever is most worth reading.

Catalogue

Five things
the grid does
besides decorate.

An informal taxonomy. None of these are exclusive to the grid; each is something the grid happens to do better than most page furniture.

i.

It establishes scale

The cell is a unit. Headlines that span six cells read as headlines without further announcement.

ii.

It admits hierarchy

Density is a free contrast. Brighter cells pull weight; dim ones recede without leaving.

iii.

It carries motion

The wave that loads the page is the same one that nominates the headline. One gesture, two readings.

iv.

It holds silence

Empty cells aren't blank — they're paused. The eye notices the rest.

v.

It survives translation

Pixels, print, projection. A rule is a rule on any substrate.

Hold still long enough,
and a background
becomes a foreground.
A working maxim
“The plainness of a ruled page is not the absence of design. It is the design, holding still long enough to be read.”
After Tschichold
Portrait · 3:4
“The best system disappears into the work you do with it. You stop noticing the lines and start noticing what they hold.”
Subject Name Designer & printer, in conversation
Cell density

Forty pixels on the right.
One hundred and sixty on the left.

The visible patch of grid is twice as dense where the eye lands, four times as sparse where it doesn't. Texture does the same work a rule of thirds would.

4×density ratio
Measures

Three figures
that hold the page together.

32columns
Tile grid
Wide enough for a comfortable headline, narrow enough that a paragraph stays in a single block.
18rows
Tile grid
A 16:9 canvas in cells of sixty pixels — the page resolves on its own diagonals.
900ms
Reveal duration
Long enough to feel composed, short enough that nobody is waiting for the slide.
Close-knit

Tight, leaning left,
56px cells, −8°.

A denser weave; the surface looks held together. The slight rotation off vertical reads as effort — like writing on a slope.

Airy

Loose, leaning right,
120px cells, +8°.

Twice the spacing, the opposite lean. The two halves never align — that mis-registration is the whole point.

Triptych

Three small inquiries,
one shared page.

i.

What it carries

A grid is a contract about where things may live. The contract is enforced by attention, not by ink.

ii.

What it costs

A rigid grid is cheap to obey and expensive to defy. The defiance is where most of the design ends up living.

iii.

What it leaves

The cells you don't fill. A reader notices a paused cell as quickly as a struck one — sooner, often.

A spread from a press proof, photographed under raking light. The grid the printer used to register the run is just visible at the edge of the bleed.

Annotation

A specimen,
with marginalia.

The artifact and the gloss share a page so the reader can compare without flipping. The image carries the evidence; the right column carries the argument.

A 50/50 split keeps neither column from dominating. The grid bridges the gap.

Sequence

Four beats,
each settling before the next.

First, 0 — 120ms

The grid notices

Cells under the headline light up at full brightness, in block-scan order.

Then, 120 — 480ms

The halo answers

Neighbouring cells fade up at a softer brightness, a slow second wave around the text.

Meanwhile, 0 — 820ms

The carriage glides

The scribe steps from the last tick to the next; the numeral crossfades in place.

Lastly, 720 — 900ms

The pearl clicks

A brief tick-pulse at the new mark. The slide is, by then, already legible.

Two stances

Architecture, or staff?

As architecture —

Load-bearing.
Visible by intention.

The grid declares itself. Margins, columns, and baseline read as structure first, content second.

Tschichold, Muöller-Brockmann, the Swiss school.

As musical staff —

Carrier.
Invisible until needed.

The grid hosts. It steps back so the reading line can phrase, accent, and breathe.

Hochuli, Bringhurst, the editorial tradition.

Method

How a page makes its case.

i.

Pause

Set the grid before setting type. Decide what the page is supposed to hold still for.

ii.

Place

Drop the headline first. Everything else negotiates with where the headline lands.

iii.

Prune

Take away one element. Then another. Stop when one more removal would lose the argument.

iv.

Print

Proof under raking light. The grid you can't see is the one the page actually used.

“What does the page
ask the reader to do?”
Discussion · 5 min
a —

The margin

Not waste. The reader's anchor: where the eye returns between lines.

b —

The baseline

Where letters sit and breathing happens. The rhythm of the page.

Schema · specimen, annotated
c —

The column

Width is a reading decision. Too wide, the eye loses the return; too narrow, the line frays.

d —

The gutter

The pause between columns. Negotiated, not measured: it is whatever silence the spread needs.
